_notice: DEMO FIXTURE. Labelled addresses are real (research/data label sets); suspect/hop addresses, tx hashes, amounts and confidences are synthetic placeholders for UI development. Not evidence.

rows.text: Automatically analyze suspect cryptocurrency wallet addresses reported during investigations on the Sahyog Platform.
rows.what: A portal posts a complaint with its wallets to the intake API over signed HTTP; one case is opened per wallet and traced without anyone touching the tool, and the result is pushed back to the portal over signed HTTP. Proven between two separate programs (the tool and a reference portal, each with its own port and store) by a conformance suite: a bad signature, an old timestamp and a replayed call are refused, and a duplicate delivery opens nothing twice.
rows.gap: SAHYOG's real interface is not public: only authorised agencies' nodal officers use the portal, and service providers are connected by arrangement with I4C. This runs against our reference portal, a separate program written from our contract, not against SAHYOG. What I4C would need to give us to connect is one page of docs/sahyog_contract.md: a base address, credentials and the field mapping.

rows.text: Automatically trace blockchain transaction paths to identify: nearest centralized exchange, custodial wallet service, or VASP receiving direct deposits from the suspect wallet.
rows.what: A wallet's money is followed hop by hop to the nearest labelled exchange, custodial wallet or swap service, in both directions. The exchange is named only when the label evidence holds; otherwise the case says the evidence is insufficient.

rows.text: Map blockchain of deposit addresses and transaction flows across multiple blockchain networks such as: Bitcoin, Ethereum, Tron, BNB Chain, Solana, Polygon, and other major chains.
rows.what: Wallets are traced on Bitcoin, Ethereum, Tron, BNB Chain, Solana and Polygon, and on Arbitrum, Base and Optimism.

rows.text: Support identification of: exchange clusters, hot wallets, deposit wallets, mixers/tumblers, DeFi bridges, and cross-chain swap services.
rows.what: Labels carry the owner and the kind of wallet (hot, cold, deposit, reserve); Bitcoin addresses are clustered by co-spending; Tron deposit addresses are derived from sweeps and scored by a measured model; mixers, bridges and swap services are recognised from labels, and a CoinJoin from the shape of the transaction.

rows.text: Integrate Sahyog with blockchain intelligence APIs and graph analytics engines.
rows.what: The tracing and attribution engine sits behind a documented HTTP API with a contract for both directions (complaints in, results and requests out, replies in). An HTTP gateway makes the outgoing calls: an API key, an HMAC signature over each call with a timestamp and a nonce, idempotency keys, retries with a pause, timeouts, and a sentence that names the host when the portal cannot be reached. It is chosen by configuration (SAHYOG_URL); with none set, a local outbox stands in and nothing leaves the machine.
rows.gap: SAHYOG's real interface is not public: only authorised agencies' nodal officers use the portal, and service providers are connected by arrangement with I4C. This runs against our reference portal, a separate program written from our contract, not against SAHYOG. What I4C would need to give us to connect is one page of docs/sahyog_contract.md: a base address, credentials and the field mapping.

rows.text: Provide automated tagging and confidence scoring for suspected VASPs.
rows.what: Each exchange a trace reaches is tagged with its owner, the kind of wallet and the label's source, and carries a confidence kept apart from how near it is; where the deposit-address model scored the wallet, the confidence uses its calibrated probability and shows the interval. The confidence is a rule-set score: measured on six chains it orders answers but is not a calibrated probability, so what is quoted is the error among named wallets at the 0.60 bar (on the model page, with the calibration measurement).

rows.text: Generate investigation-ready reports for LEAs.
rows.what: Every finished case has an A4 case file (PDF): the result, where the funds went, the flow diagram, each exchange with its evidence and transaction hashes, the flags, the risk indicators, the limits, and a provenance receipt that can be verified.

rows.text: Assist investigators in automatically routing lawful disclosure or freezing requests to the correct VASP through the SAHYOG Portal.
rows.what: Wallets are grouped under the exchange they route to; one request per exchange is drafted with its legal basis and approved by the officer. With a portal configured the approved request and its letter are submitted to it over signed HTTP and the portal's receipt is kept; the exchange's reply comes back the same way and the request is tracked to 'freeze confirmed'. If the portal does not answer, the request stays approved and unsent and says why.
rows.gap: SAHYOG's real interface is not public: only authorised agencies' nodal officers use the portal, and service providers are connected by arrangement with I4C. This runs against our reference portal, a separate program written from our contract, not against SAHYOG. What I4C would need to give us to connect is one page of docs/sahyog_contract.md: a base address, credentials and the field mapping. No request has reached a real exchange.

rows.text: visualization of fund movement
rows.what: The Hop Rail, the fund-flow graph with a replay, the timeline and the 'where the funds went' bar on every case. The graph draws the wallet's own money only, and says so in the trace's own counts: how many transfers it saw, how many it followed, and why each other wallet was not followed. The rest of what it read can be switched on as greyed context, for one wallet or for all, without changing the answer. Many small payers of one wallet are drawn as one group that opens in place. An optional 3D view shows the same picture turned.

rows.text: cross-chain transaction mapping
rows.what: Three bridge families are matched from deposit to payout through each bridge's own public index: Across, Stargate (through LayerZero Scan) and Wormhole's token bridge (through Wormholescan). The amount that arrived is read from the payout transaction on the destination chain, never taken from the bridge, and the trace goes on from the recipient there with the same rules; the crossing counts as a hop and its cost as a fee. Two recorded wallets: one followed from Ethereum onto Base through Across, and one whose USDC left Ethereum in eight Stargate deposits, seven of them followed onto Arbitrum (39,852.38 USDC sent, 39,828.50 arrived, each in about three minutes; recorded 8 Oct 2026, artifacts/crosschain/eth-stargate.json). A swap service on the path is named as a VASP and its request asks for the payout chain, address and transaction.
rows.gap: Followed: Across, Stargate, and Wormhole only when the transfer was redeemed on a chain this tool reads in an asset it follows; the one real Wormhole transfer recorded went to Kaia and is matched and named, not followed, and the token bridge pays out its own wrapped token. A Stargate deposit that waits for a shared delivery is not matched. Only flagged, with the transaction to follow by hand: Hop, Synapse, Celer, Multichain, Orbiter and the rollups' own bridges. A payout in another asset than the deposit is named but not followed. A swap service's payout cannot be matched on-chain at all: it is asked for. The Stargate wallet is a recorded test case, not yet one of the demo cases on the screen.

rows.text: risk scoring
rows.what: A score from 0 to 100 built from named red-flag indicators, each with its points and the transactions behind it. It is an indicator score, not a probability. Measured on 8 Oct 2026 on 65 wallets public sources list as illicit and 65 with a documented ordinary purpose, drawn after the points were last changed and none of them used to set them, each with its own label hidden: 22 of 65 and 2 of 65 scored High or above, all 22 through a link to another listed address. It finds a wallet that touches known bad addresses; it says nothing reliable about one that does not (9 of 10 ransomware addresses scored Low without their own label). The indicators for an address the issuer of USDT has frozen were added on 14 Oct 2026, after this measurement, and are not measured.

rows.text: identification of laundering typologies
rows.what: Peel chains, fan-out, fan-in, forwarding within minutes, round amounts, bridge hops and CoinJoin shapes are flagged, each with the wallet, the figures and the transaction hashes. Measured on 8 Oct 2026 on two sets of real listed and ordinary wallets (135, then a fresh 130): no pattern rule fired more often on the listed wallets in either (second set: peel chain 2 of 65 against 1 of 65, fan-out 6 against 17, fan-in 21 against 15, forwarding within minutes 16 against 15, round amounts 7 against 2). A flag describes how money moved and is not by itself a sign of crime, so together the five add at most 20 risk points, below Medium.

rows.text: alerting for high-risk wallets linked to ransomware, darknet, terrorism financing, or fraud ecosystems
rows.what: Labels carry threat tags from cited public sources (the OFAC SDN list, the UK Sanctions List, the EU financial sanctions list, Israel's NBCTF seizure and forfeiture orders, Ransomwhere, GraphSense TagPacks, scam lists, the block explorer's own name tags): ransomware, darknet market, terrorism financing, fraud, and the wallets of hacks and exploits. A case is screened when it is opened, a link to a tagged address is an alert that names the threat and the source, and a watched wallet raises a change on a new link or a higher risk class. A wallet none of those sources lists raises nothing: the alert is only as wide as the lists, and they are uneven by chain (the Tron tags are terrorism financing and sanctions only, 685 of them from NBCTF orders; the ransomware and darknet tags are Bitcoin; fraud is mostly Ethereum). An address several lists name shows each entry. Every case is also screened against the addresses the issuer of USDT has frozen.

rows.text: Automated identification of nearest VASP/exchange linked to unknown wallets.
rows.what: Paste a wallet and the nearest exchange comes back with its proximity and its confidence, or 'insufficient evidence' with what would change that.

rows.text: API-driven blockchain tracing and attribution support.
rows.what: Everything the interface does goes through the HTTP API (docs/api_contract.md, docs/openapi.json): open a case, read the result, the case file, the receipt.

rows.text: Multi-chain transaction analysis and visualization.
rows.what: Wallets are traced on Bitcoin, Ethereum, Tron, BNB Chain, Solana and Polygon, and on Arbitrum, Base and Optimism.

rows.text: Real-time generation of investigative intelligence.
rows.what: A trace starts the moment a wallet is submitted and the case page shows what it has read so far. Watched wallets can be traced again in the background on a schedule (VASPFUSION_WATCH_INTERVAL, seconds per wallet), each check reading the chain afresh through the shared rate limiter; a new transfer, a new exchange contact, a new link to a tagged address or a rise in risk class is raised as a change with the time of the trace that found it. Measured live, from the public chain APIs with nothing cached, one trace took a median of 11.4 s on BNB Chain, 13.0 s on Polygon, 13.4 s on Ethereum, 15.4 s on Bitcoin, 21.5 s on Solana (the six-chain benchmark) and 40.8 s on Tron (8 traces, 5.6 to 67.8 s, 8 Oct 2026; artifacts/live_timing.json). Replayed with no network, a complaint with the 12 recorded wallets went from intake to 12 results in 6.3 seconds.
rows.gap: The watcher polls: it sees a transfer at the next scheduled check, not when the block is mined, and nothing subscribes to a chain. It is off in the offline demo, which cannot reach a chain, and it has been tested on recorded responses that change between checks, not left running against live chains for days. The live times are medians of single traces through free API tiers; the Tron figure is a sample of eight.

rows.text: Risk classification of wallets and transaction flows.
rows.what: Every wallet and every case has a class (Low, Medium, High, Severe) with its reasons, and every traced transfer is classified by the indicators on it.

rows.text: Dashboard for LEAs with case-based analytics and reporting.
rows.what: Counts of cases by outcome, by chain and by risk class, the exchanges reached, requests awaiting reply and recent alerts, each counted from stored records and linked to the list behind it.

rows.text: Scalable architecture capable of handling large-volume blockchain transaction analysis.
rows.what: A batch of up to 2,000 wallets is uploaded, queued in a table that survives a restart, and traced by a pool of worker processes that share one response cache and one rate limit per provider. The officer can raise a trace's budget from 40 to 2,000 wallets. Measured on one machine: 410 cases a minute with one worker, 901 with four (artifacts/scale/metrics.json).
rows.gap: Measured on one laptop with chain responses replayed from a cache. Live, the providers' free rate limits bound the volume: one live trace took a median of 11 to 41 seconds depending on the chain, one at a time; live throughput with several workers was not measured. More than four workers gave no gain there. The case store is a single file with one writing process, and nothing was run on more than one machine (docs/scaling.md).

rows.text: reduce investigation time
rows.what: A wallet is traced, attributed and written up as a case file and a draft request without manual chain analysis. The tool's time is measured: replayed, 0.5 s a wallet; live, a median of 11 to 41 s a trace depending on the chain. A timing sheet for the same task done by hand with a block explorer, on five of the recorded wallets, is ready with its instructions (docs/manual_timing.md).
rows.gap: The manual timing is pending: nobody has filled the sheet yet, so the time the same work takes by hand is not measured and no saving is claimed. It has to be done by a person with a clock; the figures will be recorded in artifacts/manual_timing/ with who timed it, the date and the sample size.

rows.text: improve asset freezing efficiency
rows.what: A freeze can be asked for in the request (section 106 BNSS is added to the legal basis) and the request is tracked until the exchange confirms the freeze. The part this tool controls is measured: on 8 Oct 2026 one complaint with the 13 recorded wallets went from arriving to four freezing requests drafted with their letters, one per exchange, ready for the officer's signature, in 4.3 seconds (median of three runs, chain responses replayed; make freeze-readiness, artifacts/freeze_readiness.json). The dashboard shows the figure with what it does not cover. A second route, outside SAHYOG: the issuer of USDT can freeze an address. Its freeze list is read from the token contracts on Tron and Ethereum (10,674 addresses frozen at 14 Oct 2026 00:00 UTC; 100 of 100 sampled addresses gave the same answer from the contract's own call; make frozen), every case is screened against it on intake and along the traced path, and where traced USDT sits at or passed through an address outside any exchange the case offers a draft request to the issuer, citing only Tether's own published policy.
rows.gap: No real freeze was made or timed, by an exchange or by the issuer. No request of ours can reach an exchange or the issuer, so how long either takes to freeze, and whether this shortens it, is not known. Tether publishes no channel for submitting a freeze request; the draft names only the address it gives for inquiries about its policies. The 4.3 seconds replays recorded chain responses; live, each wallet's trace also waits on the public chain APIs (a median of 11 to 41 seconds by chain).

rows.text: enhance attribution capabilities
rows.what: Attribution is measured, not asserted, on six chains beside a naive baseline: 761 real wallets that paid a labelled exchange were traced with the labels one hop away hidden (Tron 280, Ethereum 213, Bitcoin 96, BNB Chain 84, Polygon 74, Solana 14). The share named wrongly is on the model page for each chain (Tron 15 of 155, Ethereum 22 of 69, Bitcoin 2 of 28, BNB Chain 0 of 19, Polygon 0 of 11, Solana 0 of 3), with the deposit-address model's calibration error and coverage.

rows.text: strengthen cross-border cybercrime investigations involving VDAs
rows.what: Foreign exchanges are named and requests are routed to them with their legal name, jurisdiction and law-enforcement channel where a source for these was found. For an exchange that no source shows as registered with FIU-IND, the desk makes a draft letter of request for a Court to issue to an authority outside India (section 112 BNSS), with the same evidence table as the domestic letter, and a case that reaches several exchanges says who to write to first, with reasons. The dashboard and each case show the traced money on a map by the country each exchange is registered in, with the source of every country.
rows.gap: The letter of request is a draft for the officer and the Court: nothing is transmitted. A cited jurisdiction is on file for 13 of the 22 exchanges in the directory, among them every exchange the recorded cases reach; Bitget's is the office location a regulator lists, not a place of incorporation. An exchange with no cited country is listed beside the map, not placed.

source: Smart India Hackathon problem statement 26182 (Ministry of Home Affairs, I4C), quoted word for word.
